title: Software & Operating Systems
summary: System vs application vs utility software, what an OS does, Windows features, and file systems. Classification (odd-one-out) questions are the most frequent pattern here.

subtopics.title: Types of software: system, application, utility
subtopics.concept:
| Class | What it does | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| System software | Runs/manages the machine itself | Operating systems (Windows, Linux, macOS, Android), device drivers, firmware/BIOS |
| Utility software | Maintains, protects, optimises | Antivirus, disk defragmenter, disk cleanup, backup tools, compressors (WinZip/7-Zip), file manager |
| Application software | User tasks | General purpose: MS Office, browsers, media players; Custom/application-specific: payroll system, railway reservation |

**Licence classes:** Freeware (free to use, source closed - Adobe Reader), Shareware (free trial, pay later - WinZip), Open source (source code available - Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox), Proprietary (paid licence - MS Office). **Firmware** is software burned into hardware (BIOS chip).

tricks.title: SUApp test
tricks.body: Ask: does it **S**erve the machine (system), **U**nclog/maintain it (utility), or do the user's **App**-job (application)? Windows = system, antivirus = utility, Excel = application.

example.solution: Utility software - it maintains disk performance.

mistakes: Counting device drivers as application software - they are system software.
Calling antivirus an operating system - it is a utility.
Assuming freeware is open source - freeware is free of cost but source stays closed.

subtopics.title: Operating system functions, types and booting
subtopics.concept:
An **Operating System** is the system software that manages hardware and provides the platform for applications.

**Functions:** process management (CPU scheduling of tasks), memory management (allocating RAM, virtual memory), file management (folders, FAT32/NTFS), device management (via drivers), security (users, passwords, permissions), user interface (GUI/CLI), error handling, networking and resource allocation. The **kernel** is the core of the OS that always stays in memory.

**Types:** single-user single-task (old DOS), single-user multi-task (Windows desktop), multi-user (UNIX/Linux servers), multiprogramming (several programs in RAM; CPU switches when one waits for I/O), multitasking, **time-sharing** (CPU time slices among users), **real-time (RTOS)** (guaranteed response within deadlines - missiles, robots, medical devices), distributed (many networked machines acting as one), embedded, mobile (Android - Linux kernel based; iOS; Windows).

**Booting** = starting the OS. **Cold boot** = power-on from off; **Warm boot** = restart without cutting power. Sequence: power-on -> **POST** (Power-On Self-Test) -> BIOS/UEFI finds the boot device -> boot loader loads the **kernel** -> login screen.

tricks.title: PMF-SUIE services
tricks.body: OS gives six services: **P**rocess, **M**emory, **F**ile, **S**ecurity, **U**I, **E**rror handling. 'Manage + platform' answers are OS; anything computing payroll is application.

example.q: Which OS service allocates RAM to programs?

tricks.title: Boot words
tricks.body: **C**old boot = **C**urrent was off (switched on from cold); **W**arm boot = **W**ithout power cut (restart). POST always comes first: 'Power On, Self-Test, then load'.

mistakes: Calling the shell/GUI the kernel - the kernel is the in-memory core; the shell is its outer interface.
Saying multiprogramming means several CPUs - it is one CPU juggling several resident programs.
Ordering the boot loader before POST - POST always runs first.

subtopics.title: Windows OS features
subtopics.concept:
Microsoft Windows (Windows 10, 2015; Windows 11, 2021) is a single-user, multitasking, GUI-based OS.

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| GUI | Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointer (WIMP) instead of typed commands |
| Multitasking | Many programs run concurrently (preemptive scheduling) |
| Plug and Play (PnP) | New hardware is detected and configured automatically |
| File Explorer (Windows Explorer) | File/folder management shell (Win+E) |
| Control Panel / Settings | System configuration (Settings app in Win 10/11) |
| Task Manager | Processes, performance, startup (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) |
| Recycle Bin | Deleted files held here; Shift+Delete skips it (permanent) |
| Device Manager | Lists/controls hardware and drivers |
| Disk Management | Partition, format drives; Disk Cleanup/Defragmenter utilities |
| Windows Defender | Built-in antivirus/firewall; Windows Update keeps patches current |
| Command Prompt / PowerShell | CLI interfaces for typed commands |
| User accounts | Administrator vs Standard; login password/PIN |
| Virtual desktops / Snap | Multiple desktops (Win+Ctrl+D); window snapping (Win+arrow) |
| OneDrive / BitLocker | Cloud sync; disk encryption (BitLocker in Pro editions) |

Accessories: Notepad (plain text), WordPad (rich text, removed in Win 11), Paint, Calculator, Snipping Tool.

tricks.title: PnP = Plug 'n' Pray-free
tricks.body: Plug and Play means the OS auto-detects and auto-configures new hardware - no driver hunt. The phrase 'automatically detected' in a question = PnP.

example.q: Windows feature that configures a newly attached printer automatically?

tricks.title: Task Manager 3-2-Esc
tricks.body: Fastest route to Task Manager: **Ctrl+Shift+Esc** (direct). Ctrl+Alt+Del only opens the security menu first. 'Direct' is what SSC tests.

example.q: Shortcut that opens Task Manager directly?

mistakes: Believing Recycle Bin catches everything - Shift+Delete bypasses it, and flash-drive deletes often skip it too.
Confusing File Explorer (files) with Internet Explorer/Edge (browser).
Thinking Notepad saves rich formatting - Notepad is plain text only.

subtopics.title: File systems and file management
subtopics.concept:
A file system defines how an OS names, stores and retrieves files on a volume.

| File system | Used by | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| FAT32 | Windows 9x, pendrives | Max file size **4 GB** (minus 1 byte); max volume ~32 GB (Windows format limit); no permissions/journaling |
| exFAT | Flash drives, cameras | Removes FAT32's 4-GB file limit; lightweight |
| NTFS | Modern Windows | Journaling (crash-safe), file/folder **permissions/encryption**, huge files, compression; default for Windows installs |
| ext4 | Linux | Journaling; default on many distros |
| APFS | macOS/iOS | Snapshots, encryption |

File management terms: file (named collection of related data), folder/directory (container), path (drive:\folders\file.ext), file name + extension (name.type), attributes (read-only, hidden, archive, system), wildcard characters **?** (one character) and ***** (any characters) used in searches. Format = preparing a disk with a file system (erases the directory, not physically shredding data).

tricks.title: FAT32's four-wall
tricks.body: **FAT32 cannot hold a single file bigger than 4 GB** - the classic exam line. NTFS breaks that wall and adds security permissions + journaling.

example.q: A 5-GB video won't copy to a FAT32 pendrive because?
example.solution: FAT32 limits file size to 4 GB; use NTFS/exFAT.

tricks.title: Wildcards
tricks.body: In Windows search, **?** masks exactly one character and ***** masks any number: `*.docx` finds all Word files, `s?t` finds sat/set/sit.

example.q: Wildcard for 'any number of characters' in file search?

mistakes: Reversing the limits: 4-GB single-file cap belongs to FAT32, not NTFS.
Saying formatting improves disk capacity - formatting only lays down the file system.
Using ? for many characters - ? is exactly one, * is any.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which of the following is NOT system software?' or options mixing an OS with apps and utilities.
pyqPatterns.approach: Tag each option: runs the machine (system), maintains it (utility), does user work (application), then pick the odd tag.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which OS component allocates memory?' / 'Plug and Play means?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the six services and Windows feature table; match the verb in the question (allocates = memory mgmt, schedules = process mgmt, detects hardware = PnP).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Cold vs warm boot', 'first step when the computer starts'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cold = power-on from off, Warm = restart; order is always POST -> boot loader -> kernel.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Maximum file size on FAT32?' / 'Which file system supports encryption?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: FAT32 = 4 GB file wall, no security; NTFS = permissions, journaling, encryption.

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following is NOT an operating system?
solvedExamples.solution: Oracle is a database management system (application software). Windows 11, Linux and Android are operating systems (Android is built on the Linux kernel).
solvedExamples.shortcut: Scan for a DBMS/browser/office-suite name hiding among OS names - DBMS, Photoshop, Chrome are never operating systems.

solvedExamples.q:
Arrange the booting steps in order:
A. POST  B. Kernel loads  C. Boot loader runs  D. Power switched on
solvedExamples.solution: Power on (D) triggers the POST self-test (A), then the firmware hands control to the boot loader (C), which loads the OS kernel (B).
solvedExamples.shortcut: POST always precedes the loader; the kernel always comes last. Only D-A-C-B satisfies both.

solvedExamples.q: Disk Defragmenter, Disk Cleanup and WinZip are examples of:
solvedExamples.solution: All three maintain or organise the system - defragmenting files, clearing junk, compressing archives - which is the definition of utility software.
solvedExamples.shortcut: If the tool's job is 'clean, compress, protect, back up', it is a utility, not an application.

solvedExamples.q:
Statement 1: NTFS supports file-level security permissions.
Statement 2: A FAT32 volume can store a single file larger than 4 GB.
solvedExamples.solution: NTFS provides per-file/folder permissions, encryption and journaling, so Statement 1 is correct. FAT32 caps any single file at 4 GB (minus 1 byte), so Statement 2 is wrong - large files need NTFS or exFAT.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Remember the 'four-wall' of FAT32; any statement letting FAT32 hold >4-GB files is false.

practice.q: Which of the following is system software?
practice.solution: Windows 11 is an operating system - system software that manages the machine. PowerPoint, Photoshop and Tally are application programs that run on top of an OS.
practice.shortcut: The OS is the platform everything else installs on; look for Windows/Linux/macOS/Android among the options.

practice.q: An antivirus program is best classified as:
practice.solution: Antivirus maintains and protects the system, which places it in utility software (along with defragmenters, backup tools, compressors).
practice.shortcut: 'Protect/maintain/clean' verbs -> utility. Antivirus is the most-asked utility example.

practice.q: The core part of an operating system that remains permanently in main memory is the:
practice.solution: The kernel is the OS core - it manages CPU, memory and devices and always stays resident in RAM. The shell is the user interface layer; BIOS is motherboard firmware; the boot sector merely starts the loading process.
practice.shortcut: Kernel = king in the castle (always resident); shell = gate you talk to.

practice.q: Restarting a computer without switching off the power is called:
practice.solution: Warm booting (restart) reloads the OS without removing power. Cold booting means starting from a fully powered-off state.
practice.shortcut: Warm = restart (machine stays 'warm'); cold = switch on from off.

practice.q: Which OS service decides which waiting program gets the CPU next?
practice.solution: Process management (scheduling) shares CPU time among ready processes. Memory management allocates RAM, file management handles storage, device management drives peripherals.
practice.shortcut: Verb match: 'gets the CPU' -> process scheduling; 'gets RAM' -> memory management.

practice.q: A real-time operating system (RTOS) is most appropriate for:
practice.solution: An RTOS guarantees a response within a strict deadline - essential in missiles, robotics, medical devices and plant control. Payroll, browsing and design have no hard deadlines.
practice.shortcut: Life-or-deadline control jobs -> RTOS; office jobs -> general-purpose OS.

options: Several programs kept in memory with the CPU switching among them
practice.solution: In multiprogramming, multiple programs reside in main memory and the single CPU switches to another whenever the current one waits (e.g. for I/O), raising CPU utilisation. It does not require multiple CPUs or users.
practice.shortcut: One CPU, many resident programs = multiprogramming; time-sliced fairness = time-sharing.

practice.q: The Windows feature that automatically detects and configures a newly connected USB printer is:
practice.solution: Plug and Play lets the OS identify new hardware, install its driver and configure it without manual setup. Hot swapping is only the connect/disconnect-while-running part; overclocking raises clock speed; mirroring is disk redundancy.
practice.shortcut: 'Automatically detects AND configures' = Plug and Play.

practice.q: Deleting a file with Shift+Delete in Windows Explorer:
options: Deletes it permanently without moving it to Recycle Bin
practice.solution: Shift+Delete bypasses the Recycle Bin and permanently deletes the file (after confirmation). Plain Delete sends it to the Recycle Bin.
practice.shortcut: Add Shift = skip the bin. That single fact answers most Recycle-Bin questions.

practice.q: Which utility shows running processes, CPU/RAM usage and startup programs in Windows?
practice.solution: Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) displays processes, performance graphs, startup impact and lets you end tasks. Device Manager lists hardware/drivers; Disk Management handles partitions; Event Viewer logs system events.
practice.shortcut: Running apps + performance = Task Manager; hardware + drivers = Device Manager.

practice.q: Notepad, the basic Windows text editor, saves files as:
practice.solution: Notepad writes plain text with no bold/italic formatting - its default extension is .txt. Formatted text needs WordPad or a word processor.
practice.shortcut: No formatting = Notepad; any option promising fonts/bold is WordPad/Word territory.

practice.q: The maximum size of a single file on a FAT32 volume is:
practice.solution: FAT32 cannot store any single file larger than 4 GB (minus 1 byte); NTFS and exFAT lift this limit. This is why pendrives formatted as FAT32 reject large videos.
practice.shortcut: The 'four-wall' of FAT32: 4 GB per file, straight recall.

practice.q: In a Windows file search, the pattern *report*.xlsx will find:
options: All .xlsx files whose names contain the word report
All files of any type containing report
practice.solution: The asterisk matches any number of characters, so *report*.xlsx matches any Excel workbook with 'report' anywhere in its name - e.g. annual-report-2026.xlsx and report-final.xlsx.
practice.shortcut: Prefix * = anything before, suffix * = anything after; .xlsx at the end restricts the type.

practice.q: Android, the mobile operating system, is built on which kernel?
practice.solution: Android uses the Linux kernel at its core with Java/Kotlin application layers on top - a standard exam fact.
